formality: Polite plain form (丁寧語, です/ます) throughout the UI. Japanese omits a second-person pronoun entirely rather than using a formal/informal 'you' distinction (no Sie/vous-style split) — never address the user with あなた. Avoid keigo (尊敬語/謙譲語); it reads as stiff and unnatural for software copy aimed at technical/pentest users.
styleNotes: 1) Use です/ます for sentences, help text and error messages; use bare noun/verb-stem forms for buttons and short labels (保存, 削除, 適用), never です/ます on a button. 2) One Japanese rendering per English term everywhere in the UI (tables, tooltips, emails, PDF exports) — never alternate synonyms for the same concept (e.g. always クラックする for 'crack', never switch to 解析する for the same action). 3) Katakana loanwords are the expected, natural register for established security/IT terms (ハッシュ, エージェント, ベンチマーク, キースペース) — do not coin native-Japanese neologisms where the katakana form is already the industry standard. 4) Keep every doNotTranslate token (NTLM, API, hashcat flags like --force, {{placeholders}}) in Latin script exactly as given; never transliterate an acronym into katakana.

hash.note: Password hash value; use ハッシュ値 in UI labels

crack.note: Canonical verb for recovering a hash's plaintext; use クラックする everywhere this term applies. Do not drift to 解析する — that belongs to unrelated 'analyze/analysis' strings (e.g. analytics features), not to this term, and mixing the two breaks consistency

cracked hashes.translation: クラック済みハッシュ

plaintext.note: Fixed from draft's keepEnglish:true: this is a fully naturalized katakana loanword with no Latin script, the same pattern as キースペース/ベンチマーク/チャンク (all keepEnglish:false) — it is not 'kept in English', it is the standard Japanese security-industry term

potfile.note: hashcat-specific filename; use as-is with lowercase 'pot'

client potfile.translation: クライアントpotファイル

association attack.translation: アソシエーション攻撃
association attack.note: Fixed from draft's '結合攻撃': that word means 'combination/joining attack' and is the term Japanese hashcat users already associate with the separate combinator attack (mode 1, -a 1), so it would misidentify this as the wrong mode. Kept as a katakana loanword for hashcat's actual association attack (mode 9, -a 9) to avoid that collision

keyspace.note: Total number of candidates; industry term in Japanese

chunk.note: Slice of keyspace for one agent

task.note: One chunk assignment on an agent

job.note: Cracking job; commonly used in Japanese UI

loopback.note: Re-running attack with newly cracked passwords

progress.note: How much of keyspace is complete

agent.note: Machine running KrakenHashes agent and hashcat

device.note: GPU/CPU on an agent; use in device listings

claim code.note: Fixed from draft's 'クレームコード': クレーム reads as 'complaint' in everyday Japanese (customer complaint, grievance) — a false friend for English 'claim'. 登録コード ('registration code') matches the actual meaning and stays clearly distinct from voucher/バウチャー

voucher.note: Same as claim code; alternate term

offline buffer.note: Grace period before agent reported offline

binary.note: hashcat binary version shown in agent/server version displays (fixed draft's nonsensical 'use lowercase in code' note — katakana has no case distinction)

client.note: Business/consulting term for the customer entity hashlists belong to — distinct from a client-server network client, which matters here since the product also has agents/server architecture (fixed draft's unclear 'MS terminology' note)

archive.note: Hide from default lists without deleting

autosave.note: Saved automatically when leaving a field

apply.note: Button: put pending changes into effect

mount.note: Attach network share to a path

threshold.note: Percentage of budget that triggers an action

drain.note: Let running work finish without starting new work; matches Kubernetes' own Japanese 'ノードをドレインする' convention

teardown.note: Fixed from draft's 'シャットダウン' ('shutdown'): that implies a reversible stop, like powering a machine off and back on. This action irreversibly destroys the cloud instance and its disk to end billing, which is a materially different and more consequential action — 破棄 ('discard/destroy') matches infrastructure-as-code usage (e.g. terraform destroy) for that distinction

two-factor authentication.note: MFA; also called 多要素認証 in modern Japanese

API key.note: Fixed from draft's keepEnglish:false, which contradicted its own note ('keep API English'): API stays in literal Latin script (never transliterated to エーピーアイ), the same pattern as potファイル/SAN/Webhook, which are all marked true in this glossary

branding.note: Custom app name, colours and logo
